l_note: Buttermilk is the low-fat, higher-protein fraction, so it carries A1 casein from A1 herds. Cow dairy from A1-herd milk carries beta-casein A1, which Gundry treats as a lectin-like offender; A2 cow milk, or goat and sheep dairy, avoids it entirely.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Milk, buttermilk, fluid, whole (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Yogurt (plain)
note: Fermented; SIGHI rates it 1 but notes it varies a lot by product.
l_note: Plain cow's yogurt is a concentrated casein food; Gundry excludes it unless it is goat, sheep or coconut. Cow dairy from A1-herd milk carries beta-casein A1, which Gundry treats as a lectin-like offender; A2 cow milk, or goat and sheep dairy, avoids it entirely. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Yogurt, Greek, plain, whole milk (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Kefir
note: Fermented dairy carrying histamine and other amines.
l_note: Cow's-milk kefir carries A1 casein despite the fermentation; goat kefir does not. Cow dairy from A1-herd milk carries beta-casein A1, which Gundry treats as a lectin-like offender; A2 cow milk, or goat and sheep dairy, avoids it entirely. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Kefir, lowfat, plain, LIFEWAY (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Quark
note: Fresh unripened cheese; rated 0.
l_note: Quark is almost pure cow casein, so the A1 issue is at its most concentrated. Cow dairy from A1-herd milk carries beta-casein A1, which Gundry treats as a lectin-like offender; A2 cow milk, or goat and sheep dairy, avoids it entirely. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Cheese, cottage, creamed, large or small curd (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Curd cheese
note: A fresh cheese; rated 0.
l_note: A fresh curd cheese is concentrated cow casein. Cow dairy from A1-herd milk carries beta-casein A1, which Gundry treats as a lectin-like offender; A2 cow milk, or goat and sheep dairy, avoids it entirely. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Soybean, curd cheese (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Cream cheese (plain)
note: Very young cheese with no ripening; rated 0 if plain and additive-free.
l_note: Cow's-milk cream cheese carries A1 casein; Gundry's substitute is a coconut- or goat-based spread. Cow dairy from A1-herd milk carries beta-casein A1, which Gundry treats as a lectin-like offender; A2 cow milk, or goat and sheep dairy, avoids it entirely. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Cheese, cream (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Mascarpone
note: Fresh cheese; rated 0.
l_note: Mostly cream and low in casein, and Italian herds are largely A2 — Gundry treats Italian dairy as acceptable.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. USDA cream cheese (4.07) adjusted toward the higher fat / lower solids-not-fat of mascarpone; no SR Legacy row.

name: Ricotta
note: Fresh whey cheese; rated 0.
l_note: Traditional ricotta is sheep whey or Italian A2 cow milk, both of which sidestep beta-casein A1.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Cheese, ricotta, whole milk (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Mozzarella
note: Rated 0 as an unripened cheese; eat it fresh, not aged or smoked.
l_note: Italian and buffalo mozzarella avoid beta-casein A1; industrial cow mozzarella from A1 herds does not.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Cheese, mozzarella, whole milk (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Cottage cheese
note: Fresh, unripened cheese in the same group as quark and curd cheese.
l_note: Cottage cheese is explicitly on the Gundry 'No' list — it is concentrated A1 cow casein. Cow dairy from A1-herd milk carries beta-casein A1, which Gundry treats as a lectin-like offender; A2 cow milk, or goat and sheep dairy, avoids it entirely. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Cheese, cottage, with vegetables (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Gouda (young)
note: Rated 0 but SIGHI advises small quantities only.
l_note: Dutch Holstein herds are A1, so young Gouda is a concentrated A1 casein food. Cow dairy from A1-herd milk carries beta-casein A1, which Gundry treats as a lectin-like offender; A2 cow milk, or goat and sheep dairy, avoids it entirely. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Cheese, gouda (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Aged Gouda
note: Ripening raises the histamine load; rated incompatible.
l_note: Aged or not, Dutch Gouda comes from A1 herds. Cow dairy from A1-herd milk carries beta-casein A1, which Gundry treats as a lectin-like offender; A2 cow milk, or goat and sheep dairy, avoids it entirely.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. USDA gouda 2.22 g carbohydrate; ageing lowers it further as lactose is fermented out.

name: Cheddar cheese (aged)
note: Aging concentrates histamine and tyramine; the older the cheese, the higher the load.
l_note: Cheddar from A1 herds is a concentrated beta-casein A1 food. Cow dairy from A1-herd milk carries beta-casein A1, which Gundry treats as a lectin-like offender; A2 cow milk, or goat and sheep dairy, avoids it entirely.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Cheese, cheddar (Includes foods for USDA's Food Distribution Program) (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Hard cheese (all well-matured cheeses)
note: SIGHI's highest cheese rating: all well-matured hard cheeses are very poorly tolerated.
l_note: Depends entirely on the herd: French and Italian hard cheeses are largely A2 and Gundry-approved, Northern-European and American ones are A1.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Cheese, parmesan, hard (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Blue cheese
note: Mold-ripened cheeses are rated incompatible with both histamine and other amines.
l_note: Cow's-milk blues carry A1 casein; sheep's-milk blues do not.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Cheese, blue (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Roquefort
note: Mold-ripened; rated incompatible.
l_note: Roquefort is sheep's milk — no beta-casein A1 at all, and one of Gundry's explicitly recommended cheeses. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Cheese, roquefort (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Brie and Camembert
note: Surface-mold-ripened cheeses fall in SIGHI's mold cheese group.
l_note: French herds are largely A2, so Brie and Camembert avoid most of the beta-casein A1 problem.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Cheese, brie (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Feta cheese
note: Brined cheese; moderately compatible with some histamine and other amines.
l_note: Real feta is sheep and goat milk, which carries no beta-casein A1.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Cheese, feta (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Fontina cheese
note: Ripened cheese; rated incompatible.
l_note: Italian Alpine cow's milk is largely A2, so Fontina avoids most of the A1 casein load.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Cheese, fontina (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Processed cheese
note: Made from ripened cheese plus melting salts; rated incompatible.
l_note: A1 casein plus emulsifying salts, and often wheat or corn starch as a bulking agent.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Ham and cheese spread (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Cheese from raw milk
note: Higher bacterial load than pasteurised-milk cheese, so higher histamine risk.
l_note: Raw-milk cheese from traditional European breeds is usually A2; from a modern Holstein herd it is not. Genuinely depends on the source.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. USDA whole-milk mozzarella as the nearest listed unaged raw-milk-style cheese; aged raw-milk cheeses run lower.

name: Egg yolk
note: The yolk alone is well tolerated.
l_note: Eggs contain no plant lectin. Gundry's only caveat is the hen's feed — pastured or omega-3 eggs avoid the corn-and-soy diet of conventional layers.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Egg, yolk, raw, fresh (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Egg white
note: Mast cell activating, especially raw, but even when cooked.
l_note: Eggs contain no plant lectin. Gundry's only caveat is the hen's feed — pastured or omega-3 eggs avoid the corn-and-soy diet of conventional layers. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Egg, white, raw, fresh (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Whole chicken egg
note: The yolk is fine; the white is the liberator. Well-cooked whole eggs are tolerated by many.
l_note: Eggs contain no plant lectin. Gundry's only caveat is the hen's feed — pastured or omega-3 eggs avoid the corn-and-soy diet of conventional layers. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Egg, whole, raw, fresh (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Quail eggs
note: Rated 0 by SIGHI.
l_note: Eggs contain no plant lectin. Gundry's only caveat is the hen's feed — pastured or omega-3 eggs avoid the corn-and-soy diet of conventional layers.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Egg, quail, whole, fresh, raw (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Duck eggs
note: Not separately listed; treated like chicken eggs because of the white.
l_note: Eggs contain no plant lectin. Gundry's only caveat is the hen's feed — pastured or omega-3 eggs avoid the corn-and-soy diet of conventional layers. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Egg, duck, whole, fresh, raw (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Rice
note: A core low-histamine staple. Refrigerate cooked rice and use within 12-24 hours.
l_prep: Rinse until the water runs clear, soak an hour, then pressure-cook; use white (hulled) rice rather than brown — the bran layer is where the lectin lives.
l_note: White rice has the lectin-bearing bran removed; brown rice keeps it and rates higher.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Wild rice, raw (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Wild rice
note: Rated 0; botanically not a true rice.
l_prep: Rinse until the water runs clear, soak an hour, then pressure-cook; use white (hulled) rice rather than brown — the bran layer is where the lectin lives.
l_note: Wild rice is on the Gundry 'No' list — it is an unhulled grass seed with the lectin-bearing hull intact. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Wild rice, raw (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Rice noodles
note: Rated 0 but slightly less well tolerated than freshly cooked rice.
l_note: Made from hulled white rice, so the lectin-bearing bran is already gone.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Rice noodles, dry (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Oats
note: Rated 0; some varieties occasionally cause flatulence.
l_note: Oats are on the 'No' list and Gundry is explicit that pressure-cooking does not knock out oat lectins. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Oats (Includes foods for USDA's Food Distribution Program) (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Quinoa
note: Rated 0, with a note that it is possibly not always well tolerated.
l_prep: Rinse repeatedly until the water runs clear, soak an hour, then pressure-cook; unrinsed quinoa keeps its full saponin-and-lectin coat.
l_note: Quinoa is a pseudo-grain on the Plant Paradox 'No' list; unrinsed it is one of the higher-lectin 'health foods'. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Quinoa, uncooked (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Millet
note: Rated 0 by SIGHI.
l_note: Millet is one of the four grains Gundry explicitly approves — it is lectin-free.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Millet, raw (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Amaranth
note: The pseudo-grain, not the azo dye of the same name; may cause diarrhea in some cases.
l_prep: Rinse thoroughly, soak, then pressure-cook, as for quinoa.
l_note: Grouped with quinoa as a high-lectin pseudo-grain, though amaranth is much less studied than quinoa and the picture is genuinely unsettled. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Amaranth grain, uncooked (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Buckwheat
note: Rated incompatible, possibly only when not thoroughly hulled.
l_prep: Soak and pressure-cook; the hull is the lectin-bearing part, so hulled groats start lower.
l_note: Buckwheat is a pseudo-grain on the Gundry 'No' list despite being gluten-free.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Buckwheat (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Corn / maize (fresh or dried)
note: Rated 0; canned corn is harder to digest.
l_note: Corn is a headline Plant Paradox offender and the lectin is not removed by ordinary cooking. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Corn, sweet, white, raw (8-20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Cornflakes
note: Rated 0 if free of malt and folic acid.
l_note: A processed corn product — the whole grain goes in, so the corn lectin comes with it. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Cereals ready-to-eat, RALSTON Corn Flakes (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Cornstarch
note: Plain starch rates 0.
l_note: Corn-derived; heavily refined, but Gundry excludes everything made from corn without exception. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Cornstarch (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Wheat
note: Uneven tolerance, mostly digestive complaints like flatulence.
l_note: Wheat germ agglutinin is the flagship dietary lectin and it is heat-stable — over 80% inactivation needs 90C for more than 10 minutes, which ordinary cooking and baking do not reach. Pressure-cooking explicitly does not fix wheat. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Wheat, durum (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Spelt
note: Rated 0; prefer old varieties over modern ATI-rich cultivars.
l_note: An ancient wheat — it carries the same heat-stable wheat germ agglutinin, and Gundry names spelt as one pressure-cooking cannot rescue. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Spelt, uncooked (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Rye
note: SIGHI notes rye is barely tolerated.
l_note: Rye carries the same heat-stable agglutinin family as wheat, and Gundry names it as one pressure-cooking cannot rescue. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Rye flour, dark (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Barley
note: Moderately compatible.
l_note: Barley carries the same heat-stable agglutinin family as wheat, and Gundry names it as one pressure-cooking cannot rescue. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Barley, pearled, raw (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Barley malt
note: Rated incompatible; a very common hidden ingredient in cereals and breads.
l_note: Malting sprouts and partly degrades the barley lectin, but a real load survives into the malt.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. malted barley syrup, maltose-dominant; the matched USDA row was pearled barley grain, a different product. Per 100 g, which is the jar rather than the meal - a normal pinch or spoonful contributes a fraction of a gram of net carbs.

name: Bread
note: Problem ingredients are malt, iodine and long yeast or sourdough fermentation times.
l_note: Baking does not destroy wheat germ agglutinin — crumb temperature never reaches the 90C-plus needed, so bread carries it through. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Bread, white wheat (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Sourdough bread
note: Long fermentation times are specifically flagged as a problem by SIGHI.
l_prep: Choose a genuinely long-fermented sourdough (24h+) made from white rather than whole-wheat flour: fermentation with the right lactobacilli cuts WGA by 35-59%, and white flour starts at roughly 4 ug/g against 30 ug/g for whole wheat.
l_note: Sourdough fermentation measurably degrades wheat germ agglutinin but does not eliminate it — this is a reduction, not a solution.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Bread, wheat (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Baked goods (general)
note: Depends on malt, iodine and fermentation time; check the ingredient list.
l_note: Wheat-flour baked goods carry heat-stable wheat germ agglutinin straight through the oven. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. category placeholder - USDA breads and cakes cluster 45-55 g.

name: Pasta (wheat)
note: Rated with wheat: uneven tolerance, mostly digestive.
l_note: Durum wheat pasta carries wheat germ agglutinin, and boiling does not reach the temperature that would inactivate it. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Pasta, dry, enriched (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Tapioca / sago
note: Rated 0 by SIGHI.
l_note: Cassava starch is on the Gundry 'Yes' list as an approved resistant starch — lectin-free.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Tapioca, pearl, dry (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Maltodextrin
note: Rated 0 by SIGHI despite the name; distinct from malt extract.
l_note: Usually corn-derived, but hydrolysed down to pure starch fragments, so essentially no lectin protein survives.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. a purified glucose polymer; USDA has no row. Value is the standard commercial spec (>=94 g available carbohydrate, no fibre).

name: Chestnut
note: Rated 0; starchy rather than nut-like in composition.
l_note: Chestnut and chestnut flour are both on the Gundry 'Yes' list — lectin-free.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Nuts, chestnuts, european, raw, peeled (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Wheat germ
note: Contains putrescine, spermine, spermidine and cadaverine.
l_note: Wheat germ is the single most concentrated source of wheat germ agglutinin there is, and WGA is heat-stable, so no preparation fixes it.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Wheat germ, crude (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Gluten (isolated)
note: Well tolerated in many cases; flatulence in some.
l_note: Gluten itself is not a lectin, but isolated vital wheat gluten carries residual heat-stable wheat germ agglutinin along with it. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Vital wheat gluten (8-20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Walnut
note: One of the worst nuts: very poorly tolerated, liberating, and rich in other amines.
l_note: Walnut is one of Gundry's recommended daily nuts — lectin-free. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Nuts, walnuts, english (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Cashew nut
note: Moderately compatible but both liberating and amine-containing.
l_prep: Roasting and long soaking lower it a level, but Gundry excludes cashews outright rather than treating them as fixable.
l_note: Cashews are seeds of a poison-ivy relative, not true nuts, and sit alongside peanuts as the highest-lectin nut-aisle item. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Nuts, cashew nuts, raw (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Peanut
note: Rated incompatible; botanically a legume.
l_note: Peanut agglutinin is well characterised and survives roasting; peanuts are legumes and Gundry excludes them entirely.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Peanuts, spanish, raw (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Peanut butter
note: Rated with peanuts; also often stored long enough to accumulate amines.
l_note: Ground roasted peanuts carry peanut agglutinin intact — roasting does not remove it.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Peanut Butter, smooth (Includes foods for USDA's Food Distribution Program) (8-20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Hazelnut
note: Moderately compatible and mildly liberating.
l_note: A true tree nut on the 'Yes' list; lectin-free.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Nuts, hazelnuts or filberts (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Almond
note: Small amounts are well tolerated; may cause sleep problems for some.
l_prep: Blanch and slip the skins off (soak overnight, peel next day), or buy blanched almonds — the lectin is in the brown skin.
l_note: Almonds with the peel on are on the 'No' list; Gundry allows them only blanched. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Nuts, almonds (8-20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Almond flour
note: Rated with almonds; a keto baking staple in moderation.
l_prep: Use blanched almond flour rather than almond meal, which is ground with the skins on.
l_note: Blanched almond flour is a Gundry-approved flour; unblanched almond meal keeps the skins and rates higher.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Nuts, almonds, blanched (8-20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Brazil nut
note: Rated 0; one or two a day is a good selenium source.
l_note: A true tree nut on the 'Yes' list; lectin-free, limited only for selenium.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Nuts, brazilnuts, dried, unblanched (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Macadamia
note: One of the few nuts rated 0 by SIGHI.
l_note: One of Gundry's recommended daily nuts — lectin-free.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Nuts, macadamia nuts, raw (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Pistachio
note: Rated 0 by SIGHI.
l_note: One of Gundry's recommended daily nuts — lectin-free.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Nuts, pistachio nuts, raw (8-20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Pine nuts
note: Moderately compatible; several species with possibly different tolerance.
l_note: A conifer seed on the 'Yes' list; lectin-free.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Nuts, pine nuts, dried (8-20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Pecan
note: Not individually listed; grouped with the poorly tolerated tree nuts like walnut.
l_note: A true tree nut on the 'Yes' list; lectin-free. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Nuts, pecans (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Nuts (general/mixed)
note: SIGHI rates 'nuts' as a group very poorly tolerated; check individual species.
l_note: Commercial mixes are built around peanuts and cashews, the two highest-lectin items in the nut aisle.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. midpoint of the USDA rows for the tree nuts in this dataset; category placeholder.

name: Sunflower seeds
note: Rated incompatible and liberating.
l_note: Sunflower seeds are explicitly on the Plant Paradox 'No' list.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Seeds, sunflower seed kernels, dried (8-20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Pumpkin seeds
note: Rated 0 by SIGHI.
l_note: Pumpkin seeds are on the 'No' list — this is the cucurbit seed itself, the lectin-bearing part of the squash. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Pumpkin, raw (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Sesame seeds
note: Moderately compatible; may cause diarrhea in some cases.
l_note: Sesame seeds and tahini are on the Gundry 'Yes' list; only a trace lectin load.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Seeds, sesame seeds, whole, dried (8-20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Chia seeds
note: Rated 0 by SIGHI.
l_note: Chia is explicitly on the Plant Paradox 'No' list despite its reputation as a health food. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Seeds, chia seeds, dried (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Flax seeds
note: Not individually rated by SIGHI; generally reported as tolerated.
l_note: Flaxseed and flax oil are both on the 'Yes' list; lectin-free.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Seeds, flaxseed (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Hemp seeds
note: The non-psychoactive subspecies is rated 0.
l_note: Hemp seed and hemp tofu are Gundry-approved protein sources — lectin-free.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Seeds, hemp seed, hulled (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Poppy seeds
note: Small amounts are well tolerated.
l_note: Trace lectin only; poppy seed is not flagged in the lectin literature.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Spices, poppy seed (8-20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Psyllium husk
note: Rated 0; useful for both constipation and diarrhea.
l_note: Purified soluble fibre husk with essentially no protein, therefore no lectin.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. ~85 g fibre per 100 g, essentially all of the carbohydrate; net carbs round to zero. No SR Legacy row.

name: Pulses (general)
note: SIGHI rates soy, beans, peas and lentils as incompatible liberators.
l_prep: Soak overnight with 2-3 water changes, then pressure-cook at high pressure for 15+ minutes; this destroys nearly all the lectin. Boiling helps but a 30-minute rolling boil is the minimum and slow-cooking at low temperature is not enough.
l_note: Legumes are the highest-lectin food class there is; raw or conventionally cooked they are the classic offenders.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. category placeholder - USDA dry mature pulses cluster 40-50 g raw.

name: Beans (dried, all types)
note: Applies to virtually all varieties; a few individual exceptions are possible.
l_prep: Soak overnight with 2-3 water changes, then pressure-cook at high pressure for 15+ minutes; this destroys nearly all the lectin. Boiling helps but a 30-minute rolling boil is the minimum and slow-cooking at low temperature is not enough.
l_note: Dried beans carry phytohaemagglutinin — kidney beans most of all, where as few as four or five undercooked beans cause acute illness.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Yardlong bean, raw (8-20 g net carbs per 100 g).

note: Rated incompatible with the other pulses.

l_note: Anchovy and salt only — no plant lectin; check cheaper brands for added wheat. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. anchovy-and-salt condiment; no USDA row. Commercial labels run 3-5 g carbohydrate per 100 ml. Per 100 g, which is the jar rather than the meal - a normal pinch or spoonful contributes a fraction of a gram of net carbs.

name: Oyster sauce
note: Shellfish-derived and fermented.
l_note: Oyster extract thickened with corn starch and cut with wheat-containing soy sauce.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. USDA fish/soy condiment sauces cluster 10-12 g; oyster sauce has no SR Legacy row. Per 100 g, which is the jar rather than the meal - a normal pinch or spoonful contributes a fraction of a gram of net carbs.

name: Hot sauce
note: Fermented chili plus vinegar; combines several triggers.
l_note: Fermented chili — a nightshade with skin and seeds ground in, though fermentation takes some edge off.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Sauce, hot chile, sriracha (8-20 g net carbs per 100 g). Per 100 g, which is the jar rather than the meal - a normal pinch or spoonful contributes a fraction of a gram of net carbs.

name: Barbecue sauce
note: Tomato, vinegar, smoke flavour and sugar together.
l_note: Tomato base with skin and seeds, plus corn syrup and often wheat-based thickeners.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Sauce, barbecue (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Salsa
note: Tomato-based with citrus and onion.
l_prep: Make it from peeled, deseeded tomatoes and peeled, deseeded peppers.
l_note: Raw tomato and raw pepper with all the skin and seeds left in — the highest-lectin form of both.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Sauce, salsa, ready-to-serve (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g). Per 100 g, which is the jar rather than the meal - a normal pinch or spoonful contributes a fraction of a gram of net carbs.

name: Pesto
note: Aged parmesan, pine nuts and often walnuts.
l_note: Basil, pine nuts, garlic, olive oil and Italian A2 parmesan are every one of them on the Gundry 'Yes' list. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Basil, fresh (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Bouillon / stock cubes
note: Almost always contains glutamate, yeast extract, meat extract and protein hydrolysates.
l_note: Stock cubes are built on hydrolysed wheat or soy protein with corn starch as a carrier.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Soup, beef broth, cubed, dry (8-20 g net carbs per 100 g). Per 100 g, which is the jar rather than the meal - a normal pinch or spoonful contributes a fraction of a gram of net carbs.

name: Yeast extract
note: Chemically converted to glutamate; a strong liberator.
l_note: Yeast is a fungus, not a plant, but the growth substrate is usually barley or corn.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Yeast extract spread (8-20 g net carbs per 100 g). Per 100 g, which is the jar rather than the meal - a normal pinch or spoonful contributes a fraction of a gram of net carbs.

name: Seasoning from hydrolysed protein
note: Contains glutamate, histamine and other amines.
l_note: Hydrolysed vegetable protein is almost always hydrolysed wheat or soy protein.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. hydrolysed vegetable protein seasoning; no USDA row. Immaterial at use level. Per 100 g, which is the jar rather than the meal - a normal pinch or spoonful contributes a fraction of a gram of net carbs.

name: Nutritional yeast
note: A deactivated yeast product high in free glutamate; commonly reported as a trigger.
l_note: Deactivated yeast is a fungus — no plant lectin. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Leavening agents, yeast, baker's, active dry (8-20 g net carbs per 100 g). Per 100 g, which is the jar rather than the meal - a normal pinch or spoonful contributes a fraction of a gram of net carbs.

name: Cocoa powder
note: Liberator with tyramine and phenylethylamine; the theobromine also inhibits DAO.
l_note: Cocoa is on the Gundry 'Yes' list; unsweetened cocoa is lectin-free. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Cocoa, dry powder, unsweetened (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g). Per 100 g, which is the jar rather than the meal - a normal pinch or spoonful contributes a fraction of a gram of net carbs.

name: Dark chocolate
note: Tyramine and phenylethylamine plus DAO-inhibiting theobromine.
l_note: Dark chocolate at 72%+ is one of Gundry's recommended daily foods. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Chocolate, dark, 45- 59% cacao solids (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Milk chocolate
note: Contains cocoa solids, so the same problems as dark chocolate plus sugar.
l_note: The cocoa is fine; the A1 milk powder that makes it milk chocolate is not.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Candies, milk chocolate (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: White chocolate
note: Mostly cocoa butter with no cocoa solids; SIGHI rates it mostly well tolerated.
l_note: White chocolate is cocoa butter plus A1 milk solids and sugar — all of the dairy problem, none of the cocoa benefit. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Candies, white chocolate (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Cocoa butter
note: Rated 0 and mostly well tolerated, unlike cocoa solids.
l_note: Pure cocoa fat with no protein; lectin-free.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. pure cocoa fat; USDA lists it at 0 g carbohydrate.

name: Leftovers (refrigerated cooked food)
note: Histamine builds as cooked food sits. SIGHI's rule: cool briefly, freeze, thaw fast, eat at once.
l_prep: Cooling cooked starches overnight converts some to resistant starch, but it does nothing to the lectin — the score depends entirely on what the meal was.
l_note: Lectin load tracks the original dish, not the reheating; this is a placeholder rating rather than a measured one.
k_note: not a food - a preparation state. Net carbs depend entirely on the dish.

name: Restaurant / canteen meals
note: Often poorly tolerated because of holding times, stocks, and hidden additives.
l_note: Restaurant kitchens run on seed oils, wheat thickeners and corn starch as a matter of course.
k_note: not a food - net carbs depend entirely on the dish.

name: Canned or semi-finished products
note: SIGHI's diet instructions rule out canned, finished and semi-finished products.
l_note: Convenience products lean on corn starch, wheat flour and soy protein as cheap structure.
k_note: not a food - a category. Net carbs depend entirely on the product.

name: Table sugar
note: Rated 0, though SIGHI still advises using it sparingly.
l_note: Refined sucrose is pure carbohydrate with no protein — the Plant Paradox objection to sugar is glycemic, not lectin.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Beets, raw (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Glucose / dextrose
note: Rated 0; pure glucose is fructose-free, but glucose syrup may not be.
l_note: Usually corn-derived, but hydrolysed to a single sugar, so no lectin protein remains.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. pure monosaccharide - 100 g carbohydrate, no fibre.

name: Fructose
note: Rated 0 for histamine, but too much causes indigestion.
l_note: A pure sugar with no protein fraction.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. pure monosaccharide - 100 g carbohydrate, no fibre.

name: Maltose
note: Pure maltose rates 0, unlike malt extract.
l_note: Derived from barley or corn starch but hydrolysed to pure sugar; no lectin protein remains.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. pure disaccharide - 100 g carbohydrate, no fibre.

name: Lactose
note: Rated 0 for histamine; a separate issue for the lactose intolerant.
l_note: Milk sugar carrying at most a trace of casein; the A1 issue is about the protein, not the sugar.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. pure disaccharide - 100 g carbohydrate, no fibre.

name: Honey
note: Rated 0 but uneven and debated; naturally contains benzoic acid.
l_note: Local and manuka honey are on the Gundry 'Yes' list in small amounts; no lectin.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Honey (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Maple syrup
note: Rated 0 by SIGHI.
l_note: Tree sap concentrate with no protein fraction.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Syrups, maple (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Agave syrup
note: Rated 0 for histamine but very high in fructose.
l_note: No lectin — Gundry's objection to agave is its fructose load.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Agave, raw (Southwest) (8-20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Caramel (browned sugar)
note: Rated 0 by SIGHI.
l_note: Browned sucrose; no protein, no lectin.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. browned sucrose; USDA granulated sugar 99.98 less the moisture caramelisation retains.

name: Stevia
note: Rated 0; a good keto-compatible sweetener.
l_note: A Gundry-approved sweetener; a purified leaf glycoside with no lectin.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. steviol glycosides are non-nutritive; bulked tabletop products carry the bulking agent, not the sweetener.

name: Xylitol
note: Rated 0 by SIGHI.
l_note: A Gundry-approved sweetener; a purified sugar alcohol, usually from corn cobs or birch, with no lectin protein.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. sugar alcohol - excluded from net carbs by the definition used here. Note: xylitol is roughly 60% as glycaemic as sucrose, so 'zero net' overstates it.

name: Erythritol
note: A sugar alcohol in the same family as the SIGHI-tolerated polyols.
l_note: A Gundry-approved sweetener; fermented from glucose and purified, so no lectin protein remains.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. sugar alcohol, essentially unmetabolised and excreted unchanged; the one polyol where zero net is uncontroversial.

name: Sorbitol
note: Rated 0 for histamine; may cause digestive upset in quantity.
l_note: A purified sugar alcohol with no protein.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. sugar alcohol - excluded by definition. Partially absorbed; a substantial dose does raise blood glucose.

name: Mannitol
note: Rated 0 by SIGHI.
l_note: A purified sugar alcohol with no protein.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. sugar alcohol - excluded by definition. Poorly absorbed.

name: Sucralose
note: Explicitly named as the tolerated artificial sweetener.
l_note: A synthetic molecule — no plant protein; Gundry's objection is microbiome disruption.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. the sweetener itself is non-nutritive. USDA's 91.17 g figure is the maltodextrin BULKING AGENT in packet form - a packet is ~1 g, so ~0.9 g carbohydrate per packet.

name: Artificial sweeteners (general)
note: Rated 1 as a group; SIGHI notes sucralose specifically is tolerated.
l_note: Synthetic sweeteners contain no plant protein and therefore no lectin.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. non-nutritive; carbohydrate in tabletop products is the bulking agent, not the sweetener.

name: Malt extract
note: Rated incompatible; a common hidden sweetener in cereals and drinks.
l_note: Concentrated barley malt carries a real share of the grain's lectin through into the syrup.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. malt syrup is maltose-dominant at roughly 71 g carbohydrate per 100 g; no SR Legacy row for the extract. Per 100 g, which is the jar rather than the meal - a normal pinch or spoonful contributes a fraction of a gram of net carbs.

name: Palm sugar
note: SIGHI gives no firm rating for palm sugar.
l_note: Concentrated palm sap; no protein, no lectin. Gundry's objection to coconut sugar is glycemic.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. predominantly sucrose; USDA granulated sugar is 99.98. Palm sugar carries some moisture and minerals.

name: Monk fruit sweetener
note: Not listed by SIGHI; generally reported as tolerated like stevia.
l_note: A Gundry-approved sweetener; a purified fruit glycoside with no lectin.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. mogrosides are non-nutritive. Commercial blends are mostly erythritol, also counted as zero net.

name: Tap water
note: Rated 0 by SIGHI.
l_note: Water contains no plant material at all.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Water convolvulus,raw (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Still mineral water
note: Rated 0 by SIGHI.
l_note: Water contains no plant material at all.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. water.

name: Carbonated water
note: Carbonic acid is a mild short-lived liberator; symptoms pass quickly.
l_note: Water contains no plant material at all.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. water.

name: Coffee
note: Caffeine stimulates nerves and bowel, which can be mast cell activating.
l_note: Coffee is on the Gundry 'Yes' list; the roasted seed extract carries no lectin.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Beverages, coffee, brewed, prepared with tap water (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Espresso
note: Better tolerated than filter coffee but still caffeinated.
l_note: Coffee is on the Gundry 'Yes' list; no lectin in the extract.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Beverages, coffee, brewed, espresso, restaurant-prepared (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Black tea
note: Contains histamine and blocks DAO; a double problem.
l_note: Black tea is a leaf infusion — Gundry allows tea of all types, and there is no lectin in the brew. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Beverages, tea, black, brewed, prepared with tap water (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Green tea
note: A DAO blocker despite being only moderately incompatible for histamine.
l_note: Green tea is a leaf infusion — Gundry allows tea of all types, and there is no lectin in the brew.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Beverages, tea, green, brewed, regular (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Mate tea
note: A DAO blocker.
l_note: Mate is a leaf infusion — Gundry allows tea of all types, and there is no lectin in the brew.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Beverages, tea, herb, other than chamomile, brewed (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Chamomile tea
note: Rated 0 by SIGHI.
l_note: Chamomile tea is a leaf infusion — Gundry allows tea of all types, and there is no lectin in the brew.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Beverages, tea, herb, brewed, chamomile (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Peppermint tea
note: Rated 0 by SIGHI.
l_note: Peppermint tea is a leaf infusion — Gundry allows tea of all types, and there is no lectin in the brew.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Peppermint, fresh (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Rooibos tea
note: Rated 0; check blends for added orange zest and other triggers.
l_note: Rooibos tea is a leaf infusion — Gundry allows tea of all types, and there is no lectin in the brew.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Beverages, tea, herb, other than chamomile, brewed (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Sage tea
note: Rated 0 by SIGHI.
l_note: Sage tea is a leaf infusion — Gundry allows tea of all types, and there is no lectin in the brew.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Beverages, tea, herb, other than chamomile, brewed (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Nettle tea
note: Moderately compatible; the plant itself contains histamine.
l_note: Nettle tea is a leaf infusion — Gundry allows tea of all types, and there is no lectin in the brew.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Beverages, tea, herb, other than chamomile, brewed (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Herbal tea blends (medicinal)
note: Complex multi-herb mixtures are often poorly tolerated for reasons not yet identified.
l_note: Herbal tea is a leaf infusion — Gundry allows tea of all types, and there is no lectin in the brew.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Beverages, tea, herb, other than chamomile, brewed (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Kombucha
note: Fermented tea: histamine from fermentation plus the DAO-blocking tea base.
l_note: Fermented tea; low-sugar kombucha is explicitly on the Gundry 'Yes' list. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. fermented tea; no USDA row. Commercial labels run 2-6 g per 100 ml depending on residual sugar.

name: Energy drinks
note: The theobromine content inhibits the DAO enzyme.
l_note: Corn-syrup sweetened but otherwise a synthetic drink; no meaningful lectin protein.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Beverages, Energy drink, RED BULL (8-20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Cola drinks
note: Rated 1; caffeine plus carbonation.
l_note: High-fructose corn syrup is fully hydrolysed sugar, so no corn lectin protein comes through.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Beverages, carbonated, cola, regular (8-20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Soft drinks / soda
note: Depends on the ingredients; carbonation adds a short-lived liberator effect.
l_note: Corn-syrup sweetened; the sugar carries no lectin protein.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Beverages, carbonated, cola, regular (8-20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Lemonade
note: Depends on the ingredients; citrus versions are worse.
l_note: Sugar and citrus; no meaningful lectin.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Lemonade, powder, prepared with water (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Elderflower cordial
note: Rated 0 by SIGHI.
l_note: Flower infusion and sugar; no lectin.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. as-served dilution of a ~60 g/100 ml syrup at roughly 1:4; the concentrate figure would overstate a glass fourfold.

name: Cranberry juice
note: Rated 0 by SIGHI.
l_note: Berry juice; lectin-free.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Cranberries, raw (8-20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Apple juice
note: Not separately listed; rated with apple, which is 0.
l_note: Apple juice carries only the trace lectin of the fruit.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Babyfood, juice, apple (8-20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Tomato juice
note: Rated incompatible and liberating, like tomato itself.
l_prep: Only home-made from peeled, deseeded tomatoes will help; commercial juice is pressed from whole fruit.
l_note: Commercial tomato juice is whole tomato including skin and seeds — the highest-lectin part of the fruit, in liquid form.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Tomato juice, canned, without salt added (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Oat milk
note: Often slightly histamine-containing because it is enzymatically fermented.
l_note: Oat milk is a whole-oat extract and Gundry is explicit that oat lectins are not removed by cooking. Scores low for histamine but high for lectins — one of the main conflicts between the two protocols.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Oats (Includes foods for USDA's Food Distribution Program) (over 20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Rice milk
note: Often slightly histamine-containing because it is enzymatically fermented.
l_note: Made from hulled white rice, so the lectin-bearing bran is already gone.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Beverages, rice milk, unsweetened (8-20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Soy milk
note: Rated incompatible with the other soy products.
l_note: A whole-soybean extract carrying soybean agglutinin; Gundry excludes soy milk outright.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. USDA unsweetened soy milk; the matched row was an imitation non-soy milk.

name: Almond milk (unsweetened)
note: Rated with almonds at 1; check for carrageenan and other additives.
l_note: Commercial almond milk is made from blanched almonds and heavily diluted, so very little lectin comes through.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Beverages, almond milk, unsweetened, shelf stable (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Coconut milk beverage
note: Rated with coconut at 0; check for gums and stabilisers.
l_note: Coconut is a Gundry staple; the milk beverage is lectin-free.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Nuts, coconut milk, raw (liquid expressed from grated meat and water) (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Hot chocolate
note: Cocoa-based, so liberating, amine-rich and DAO-inhibiting.
l_note: The cocoa is fine; the A1 milk it is made with is the problem.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. USDA cocoa-and-sugar mix prepared with milk; the sugar dominates.

name: Coconut water
note: Not separately listed; grouped with coconut at 0.
l_note: Coconut water contains no lectin.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Nuts, coconut water (liquid from coconuts) (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Alcohol (pure ethanol)
note: Ethanol itself is both a liberator and a DAO blocker, independent of any histamine content.
l_note: Pure ethanol contains no protein of any kind. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. ethanol is not a carbohydrate. It still supplies 7 kcal/g and suppresses ketone production while it is being cleared.

name: Alcoholic beverages (general)
note: Rated 3 across the board: histamine, other amines, liberator and DAO blocker.
l_note: Depends entirely on the base: distilled spirits and wine are lectin-free, beer and grain-based drinks are not.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Alcoholic beverage, rice (sake) (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Red wine
note: The classic worst case: high histamine, tyramine, liberating, and DAO-blocking.
l_note: Red wine is explicitly Gundry-approved at six ounces daily — grape ferment carries no lectin. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Vinegar, red wine (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: White wine
note: Lower in histamine than red wine but still a liberator and DAO blocker.
l_note: Grape ferment with no protein fraction; lectin-free. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Alcoholic beverage, wine, table, white (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Rosé wine
note: Rated 2 by SIGHI, between white and red wine.
l_note: Grape ferment with no protein fraction; lectin-free. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Alcoholic beverage, wine, table, all (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Histamine-free wine
note: Under 0.1 mg/l histamine, but still contains alcohol and sulfite.
l_note: Grape ferment with no protein fraction; lectin-free.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Alcoholic beverage, wine, table, white (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Champagne
note: Rated very poorly tolerated: fermented, amine-rich, liberating and DAO-blocking.
l_note: Champagne is explicitly on the Gundry 'Yes' list; no lectin. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. brut sparkling wine; USDA table wine (2.72) less the lower residual sugar of a brut dosage.

name: Beer
note: Yeast-fermented with histamine, other amines, plus the alcohol effects.
l_note: Beer is a barley extract, often with wheat or corn adjuncts, and brewing does not remove the grain lectin.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Alcoholic beverage, beer, regular, all (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Wheat beer
note: Grouped with beer; unfiltered yeast beers are often reported as worse.
l_note: Wheat beer is a liquid wheat extract, and wheat germ agglutinin is heat-stable through the brew.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Alcoholic beverage, beer, regular, all (3-8 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Brandy
note: Rated 2 by SIGHI.
l_note: Distilled from grapes — distillation leaves all protein behind, so no lectin survives. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Alcoholic beverage, distilled, all (gin, rum, vodka, whiskey) 86 proof (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Rum
note: Rated 2 by SIGHI.
l_note: Distilled from cane; no protein survives distillation. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Alcoholic beverage, distilled, all (gin, rum, vodka, whiskey) 86 proof (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Clear spirits
note: Colourless spirits are the least bad option, but the ethanol effects remain.
l_note: Distillation leaves protein behind entirely, so even grain spirits emerge lectin-free. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Alcoholic beverage, distilled, all (gin, rum, vodka, whiskey) 86 proof (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Dark / cloudy spirits
note: Cloudy or coloured spirits are rated 3, higher than clear ones.
l_note: Gundry allows an ounce of dark spirits daily; distillation removes all protein regardless of the grain base. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Alcoholic beverage, distilled, all (gin, rum, vodka, whiskey) 86 proof (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Liqueur
note: Alcoholic plus usually fruit, cocoa or dairy additions.
l_note: The spirit base is lectin-free; added cream, corn syrup or grain infusions contribute a small load.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. sugar-forward spirits; varies enormously by product - treat as indicative only.

name: Cider
note: A fermented fruit alcohol; grouped with the fermented alcoholic beverages.
l_note: Fermented apple juice with no protein fraction; lectin-free. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. dry cider; no USDA row for the drink. Sweet ciders run substantially higher.

name: Sake
note: A fermented rice alcohol; grouped with the other fermented drinks.
l_note: Brewed from polished rice with the lectin-bearing bran already milled away.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. brewed rice wine, ~5 g residual carbohydrate per 100 ml; the matched row was wild rice grain.

name: Monosodium glutamate
note: Rated incompatible and liberating; the flagship flavour enhancer to avoid.
l_note: Monosodium glutamate is a purified amino acid salt fermented from starch — no protein, therefore no lectin. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. an amino-acid salt - no carbohydrate.

name: Glutamates (E620-E625)
note: The whole glutamate family is rated incompatible and liberating.
l_note: Glutamate salts is a purified amino acid salt fermented from starch — no protein, therefore no lectin. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. amino-acid salts - no carbohydrate.

name: Sulfites (E220-E228)
note: All sulfites are rated incompatible liberators; common in wine and dried fruit.
l_note: Sulfites is a synthetic or purified compound with no plant protein and therefore no lectin. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. preservative salts - no carbohydrate, dosed in milligrams.

name: Benzoates (E210-E213)
note: Preservatives rated incompatible and liberating.
l_note: Benzoates is a synthetic or purified compound with no plant protein and therefore no lectin. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. preservative salts - no carbohydrate, and used in milligrams.

name: Sorbates (E200-E203)
note: Preservatives rated incompatible and liberating.
l_note: Sorbates is a synthetic or purified compound with no plant protein and therefore no lectin. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. preservative salts - no carbohydrate, used in milligrams.

name: Tartrazine
note: An azo dye rated very poorly tolerated and strongly liberating.
l_note: Tartrazine is a synthetic or purified compound with no plant protein and therefore no lectin. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. azo colourant - no carbohydrate, dosed in milligrams.

name: Sunset yellow FCF
note: An azo dye rated very poorly tolerated and strongly liberating.
l_note: Sunset yellow FCF is a synthetic or purified compound with no plant protein and therefore no lectin. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. azo colourant - no carbohydrate, dosed in milligrams.

name: Allura red
note: An azo dye rated incompatible and liberating.
l_note: Allura red is a synthetic or purified compound with no plant protein and therefore no lectin. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. azo colourant - no carbohydrate, used in milligrams.

name: Annatto
note: A natural colour that is nonetheless rated incompatible and liberating.
l_note: A purified carotenoid pigment extracted from achiote seed; the protein is left behind. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. a carotenoid colourant used in fractions of a gram; the matched USDA row was a seasoning mix, not annatto.

name: Carrageenan
note: Rated incompatible and liberating; a very common thickener in creams and plant milks.
l_note: A purified seaweed polysaccharide — no lectin, though Gundry flags carrageenan separately as a gut irritant. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. a non-digestible seaweed polysaccharide, counted as fibre.

name: Locust bean gum
note: Rated incompatible and liberating; often paired with carrageenan in cream.
l_note: Carob is a legume, and locust bean gum is milled seed endosperm rather than a fully purified extract, so a trace of the family's protein comes with it.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. non-digestible galactomannan, counted as fibre.

name: Guar gum
note: Moderately compatible but still a mild liberator.
l_note: Guar is a legume; the gum is milled endosperm, so a trace of legume protein comes through.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. non-digestible galactomannan, counted as fibre.

name: Gum arabic
note: Moderately compatible but still a mild liberator.
l_note: Acacia tree exudate rather than seed material; a purified polysaccharide with no lectin.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. non-digestible polysaccharide, counted as fibre.

name: Xanthan gum
note: One of the few gums rated 0 by SIGHI.
l_note: A bacterial fermentation polysaccharide — the corn glucose substrate is consumed and no lectin protein remains.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. non-digestible polysaccharide, counted as fibre.

name: Pectin
note: Rated 0 by SIGHI.
l_note: A purified citrus or apple polysaccharide with no protein fraction.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Pectin, liquid (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Lecithin
note: Rated 0 by SIGHI, mostly soya lecithin in practice.
l_note: Usually soy lecithin — a refined phospholipid with only trace protein; sunflower lecithin is the common substitute.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. a phospholipid - no meaningful carbohydrate, used in fractions of a gram.

name: Citric acid
note: Rated 1 and debated; industrially made from mould, not from lemons.
l_note: Produced by Aspergillus fermentation, usually on corn glucose; the finished acid contains no protein.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. an organic acid - no carbohydrate.

name: Ascorbic acid / vitamin C
note: Lowers histamine levels but is also a weak DAO inhibitor: helpful in MCAS, debatable in HIT.
l_note: A purified vitamin, typically corn-derived, containing no protein.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. a vitamin dosed in milligrams; immaterial.

name: Baking soda
note: Rated 0 by SIGHI.
l_note: A mineral salt with no plant material.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Leavening agents, baking soda (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Sodium nitrite
note: Rated 0 as an additive itself; the cured meats it appears in are the real problem.
l_note: A mineral salt with no plant material.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. a curing salt - no carbohydrate, dosed in milligrams.

name: BHA / BHT
note: Antioxidant preservatives rated incompatible and liberating.
l_note: Synthetic antioxidants with no plant protein. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. synthetic antioxidants - no carbohydrate, dosed in milligrams.

name: Quinine
note: Rated incompatible; the reason tonic water is a problem drink.
l_note: A purified cinchona bark alkaloid; no lectin. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Beverages, carbonated, tonic water (8-20 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: Flavourings (unspecified)
note: This can be anything and is mostly not well tolerated.
l_note: Unspecified flavourings are usually purified extracts, but wheat- and corn-derived carriers are common and undeclared.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. used in fractions of a gram; immaterial regardless of composition.

name: Salicylic acid / salicylates
note: Rated incompatible and liberating; naturally present in many plants.
l_note: A purified plant acid, not a protein — no lectin content. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. an organic acid - no carbohydrate.

name: Yeast (baker's or brewer's)
note: Well tolerated under perfect hygiene; long dough fermentation times are the problem.
l_note: Yeast is a fungus, not a plant; no plant lectin.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Leavening agents, yeast, baker's, active dry (8-20 g net carbs per 100 g). Per 100 g, which is the jar rather than the meal - a normal pinch or spoonful contributes a fraction of a gram of net carbs.

name: Iodine
note: Rated very poorly tolerated and strongly liberating.
l_note: A mineral element; no plant material. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. a mineral dosed in micrograms.

name: Potassium iodide / iodate
note: The iodine additives in iodized salt; strongly liberating.
l_note: A mineral salt; no plant material. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. a mineral salt dosed in micrograms.

name: Folic acid
note: Rated incompatible and liberating; debated, possibly because of its glutamic acid moiety.
l_note: A synthesised vitamin with no plant protein. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. a vitamin dosed in micrograms.

name: Theobromine
note: A direct DAO inhibitor; the reason cocoa and energy drinks are flagged.
l_note: A purified cocoa alkaloid; no lectin. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. an alkaloid - no carbohydrate.

name: Vitamin E (tocopherols)
note: Rated 0 by SIGHI.
l_note: Mixed tocopherols are usually extracted from soybean oil; the purified vitamin carries no meaningful protein, but the soy origin is worth knowing.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. a fat-soluble vitamin dosed in milligrams.

name: Algae supplements
note: All algae and algae derivatives are rated 3 and liberating; extremely iodine-rich.
l_note: Algae are not land plants; spirulina and chlorella carry no dietary lectin concern. Flagged as a histamine problem yet essentially lectin-free — the two protocols disagree here.
k_note: USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy: Seaweed, spirulina, raw (under 3 g net carbs per 100 g).

name: DAO enzyme supplement
note: Supplemental DAO is the standard support product, not a trigger; taken before meals.
l_note: Traditionally made from pig kidney extract, which is lectin-free, but several newer products are pea-sprout derived — a legume source worth checking on the label.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. an enzyme capsule; carbohydrate is capsule excipient only.

name: Vitamin B6
note: A cofactor for DAO rather than a trigger; not rated as a problem by SIGHI.
l_note: A synthesised vitamin with no plant protein.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. a vitamin dosed in milligrams.

name: Quercetin
note: A mast cell stabiliser rather than a trigger; not rated as a problem by SIGHI.
l_note: A purified flavonoid, often sourced from Sophora japonica (a legume) but purified past any protein content.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. a flavonoid dosed in milligrams.

name: Probiotic supplements (mixed strains)
note: Some strains produce histamine; strain choice matters a great deal.
l_note: The bacteria are irrelevant; the carrier is usually corn maltodextrin or inulin, which carries essentially no lectin.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. capsule excipient only; some products use a prebiotic fibre carrier.

name: Collagen peptides
note: A protein hydrolysate; grouped with gelatin, which SIGHI rates 1 and controversial.
l_note: Hydrolysed animal collagen; no plant material at all.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. hydrolysed protein - USDA unsweetened gelatin powder is 0 g carbohydrate.

name: Whey protein powder
note: Plain whey rates 0, but processed powders often carry additives and flavourings.
l_note: Whey is the non-casein milk fraction, so it largely sidesteps the beta-casein A1 question — concentrates carry more residual casein than isolates.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. whey concentrate typically 6-10 g carbohydrate per 100 g as residual lactose; isolates are near zero.

name: Vinegar-preserved products (general)
note: Vinegar preservation is on SIGHI's avoid list for the elimination phase.
l_prep: Peel and deseed the vegetables before pickling; cucumbers and peppers are the usual base.
l_note: Lectin load depends on what was pickled, and it is usually cucumbers, peppers or onions — the first two being cucurbit and nightshade.
k_note: No direct USDA entry. USDA pickled vegetables cluster 2-4 g; a category placeholder.

name: Smoked products (any)
note: Any smoking process is rated 3 by SIGHI, whether meat or fish.
l_note: Smoking itself adds nothing; the score depends on whether the smoked item is animal (lectin-free) or grain-based.
k_note: not a food - a preparation state. Net carbs depend on what was smoked.
